items.headline: OpenAI raises bug bounty rewards for security researchers
items.summary: OpenAI is increasing payouts under its Security Bug Bounty programme and adding bonuses tied to report quality, researcher loyalty and priority campaigns. The programme pays independent researchers who find and report vulnerabilities in OpenAI products and services.
items.why: Bigger rewards pull more skilled researchers toward finding flaws in widely used AI systems before attackers do.

items.headline: Anthropic adds Claude Code limits aimed at game cloning
items.summary: Anthropic has confirmed new restrictions in Claude Code that stop the tool from reproducing existing video games, after its Opus 5.5 model began blocking game recreation requests. Some users report that generic reverse engineering tasks are also being blocked, and an Anthropic employee said the company is iterating to find the right balance.
items.why: It is a live example of a model maker enforcing copyright limits inside a coding tool, with false positives already hitting legitimate work.

items.headline: Experiment backs a route to more error resistant quantum information storage
items.summary: Researchers have produced experimental support for the theoretical basis of topological quantum computing, an approach that stores information in special quantum states expected to be more resistant to local disturbances. The work addresses one of the field's core problems: how easily quantum information degrades.
items.why: If topological approaches hold up, they could reduce the error correction burden that dominates quantum hardware design today.

items.headline: AWS makes Step Functions callable as agent tools
items.summary: In its weekly roundup, AWS notes that Step Functions, its workflow service spanning more than 220 AWS services, can now be handed to AI agents as a tool. Workflows that teams already run and trust become callable by agents without being rewritten.
items.why: It shows cloud platforms adapting established automation for agents rather than replacing it.

items.headline: Developers choose smaller AI models on purpose, and report better results
items.summary: The New Stack reports that some development teams are deliberately downgrading the AI models they use for coding work, and finding the results better for their purposes. The smaller setups can be cheaper and easier to control for the tasks these teams run most.
items.why: Model choice is becoming an engineering decision about fit and cost, not a race to the most powerful model.

items.headline: Microsoft: real world exploitation concentrates in a small set of vulnerabilities
items.summary: Microsoft's analysis of real world attacks finds that exploitation concentrates in a small, high impact subset of known vulnerabilities. It advises defenders to prioritise patching by exploitation likelihood, exposure and potential blast radius, rather than by severity score alone.
items.why: It gives security teams an evidence based order for patching when they cannot patch everything at once.

items.headline: Apple home robot reported for 2027 at around $1,000
items.summary: Ars Technica reports that Apple is preparing a roaming home robot for 2027, priced at about $1,000, with FaceTime and smart home controls among its functions. The device is reported to have backing from CEO John Ternus and a limited initial feature set.
items.why: It puts Apple into home robotics, a new product category for the company, at a four figure price point.

items.headline: Russia plans underground data centres after Ukrainian drone strikes
items.summary: Ars Technica reports that Ukrainian drone strikes on exposed Russian infrastructure have prompted Russian plans to move data centres underground. Russia's Digital Development Ministry has confirmed, as reported by Kommersant, that it completed drone protection recommendations for data centres, covering underground siting for the most critical sites, and sent them to the relevant organisations.
items.why: The conflict is directly reshaping where and how a major state builds and protects its data centre capacity.

items.headline: DeepMind applies AI agents to chemistry and drug discovery workflows
items.summary: Google DeepMind describes agentic cheminformatics built with its Antigravity platform and a set of Cheminformatics Skills. The system searches compounds and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles, a class of molecules used in drug design.
items.why: It is a concrete case of agents doing specialist scientific work rather than only answering questions.

items.headline: New benchmark finds frontier models lose track of changing facts in long documents
items.summary: Allen AI's StateBench tests how well language models track information that changes across long documents, across four levels of difficulty. Frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 handled simple updates but fell to 13 percent accuracy or lower on the hardest problems at the longest lengths, while recurrent and hybrid architectures generalised further when trained on the task.
items.why: Long document and agent work depends on exactly this state tracking, so the failure mode matters well beyond the benchmark.

items.headline: OpenAI shows ChatGPT and Codex in engineering work for the physical world
items.summary: OpenAI describes how engineers are using ChatGPT and Codex to speed up CAD work, PCB design, simulation and related workflows. The examples take the tools beyond software code into hardware engineering processes.
items.why: Adoption in physical engineering widens the market for AI assistants beyond software teams.

items.headline: Universal Quantum unveils a foundry made trapped ion processor built for modular scaling
items.summary: Universal Quantum has launched the iQPU, a trapped ion processor fabricated in a foundry, with control electronics integrated on chip. Its UQConnect interconnect is designed to link multiple modules, and the processors are destined for two quantum computers being built for the German Aerospace Center.
items.why: Foundry fabrication and modular links are two of the practical steps needed to scale trapped ion machines.

items.headline: One extra measurement cuts qubit errors by more than half in Regensburg experiment
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Regensburg and their international partners showed that a single additional measurement before a series of quantum operations reduced the qubit error rate by more than half. The results were published in Applied Physics Reviews.
items.why: Low cost error reduction matters because error correction overhead decides how large a useful quantum machine must be.

items.headline: Azure previews an MCP gateway for its container application gateway
items.summary: Microsoft has put an MCP gateway for Application Gateway for Containers into public preview, adding a Model Context Protocol route type. Platform teams can publish MCP servers behind one hostname while centralising TLS, token validation and firewall controls.
items.why: Gateways are becoming the control point where enterprises govern agent traffic.

items.headline: Nammu21 runs syndicated loan automation on Google Cloud's ledger in a proof of concept
items.summary: Fintech firm Nammu21 worked with Google Cloud to structure syndicated loan agreements as smart contracts on the Google Cloud Universal Ledger. The proof of concept automates the loan lifecycle in a market where settlement currently takes weeks of manual processing.
items.why: It tests ledger technology on a real, high value financial workflow rather than a pilot in isolation.

items.headline: Microsoft tracks fake download campaign spreading trojanised installers
items.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence is tracking a campaign that uses trojanised Inno installers, spread through fake download pages, to deliver monetisation payloads. Microsoft published detection and investigation guidance covering the complete installer session.
items.why: Fake installers remain one of the most reliable ways attackers reach ordinary users and company machines.

items.headline: Quint Computing raises €9.1 million seed round for hardware level quantum error correction
items.summary: Quint Computing has secured €9.1 million (10.2 million US dollars) in seed funding plus a €2.2 million European Innovation Council Pathfinder grant. The company says its architecture aims to reduce physical error correction overhead by up to 100 times, using continuous electrical control in superconducting circuits.
items.why: Error correction is where quantum hardware economics are decided, and investors are funding it at the hardware layer.

items.headline: IQM calls for an EU Quantum Act with dedicated qubit foundries

sources.label: IQM (the report: Quantum Is Europe's Second Chance)

items.summary: In a report titled Quantum Is Europe's Second Chance, IQM Quantum Computers calls on the EU to pass a Quantum Act. It proposes dedicated qubit foundries, more late stage growth capital and DARPA style procurement, arguing that Europe is strong in public investment and deployments but weaker in venture capital, chip manufacturing and regulatory speed.
items.why: The proposal shows industry shaping the EU quantum policy agenda before legislation is drafted.

items.headline: OpenAI launches Images 2.6 with faster generation and GIF creation
items.summary: OpenAI's Images 2.6 brings faster image generation, GIF creation, more precise editing and new API controls. It is available across ChatGPT, Codex and the API.
items.why: Image generation is shipping as a product feature with controls developers can build on, not only as a model demonstration.

items.headline: OpenAI pipeline finds and patches 948 Linux kernel privilege flaws
items.summary: OpenAI built an autonomous pipeline that found, validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel. The work is presented as defensive security research carried out at machine scale.
items.why: It is a measurable example of AI systems doing vulnerability research end to end.

items.headline: AWS shows decision models plugged into Bedrock AgentCore agent evaluations
items.summary: An AWS Machine Learning Blog post shows how two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, connect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations through code based evaluators. Decision models answer the narrow, repeatable evaluation questions that come up when testing AI agents.
items.why: Agent evaluation tooling is being built into the major cloud AI platforms as a standard part of the stack.

items.headline: IBM Quantum and QuICS use AI agents to find over 500 magic state factory designs
items.summary: IBM Quantum and University of Maryland QuICS researchers used AI agents with deterministic solvers to discover more than 500 new magic state factories. These produce the non Clifford states that fault tolerant quantum computers need, with significantly lower resource requirements, and the detailed circuit models are openly accessible.
items.why: Magic state production is a major cost centre in fault tolerant designs, so cheaper factories change machine economics.

items.headline: Superinductor built inside a silicon chip in a commercial CMOS process
items.summary: A study in Nature Electronics by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware group, Quantum Motion and UK partners introduces a superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit. The device was fabricated in a commercial CMOS process, the same family of processes used for ordinary chips.
items.why: Components made in standard chip processes are easier to manufacture at scale for quantum hardware.

items.headline: CQMTEK raises more than $15 million to expand quantum measurement manufacturing
items.summary: CQMTEK, the brand of Guoce Quantum Technology (Zhejiang) Co., Ltd, has raised more than 100 million yuan, about 15 million US dollars, the company said. The funding is for expanding manufacturing and commercial applications of its quantum precision measurement products.
items.why: Quantum sensing and measurement is drawing commercial funding alongside computing, with manufacturing scale as the goal.

items.headline: IonQ completes $1.15 billion acquisition of security firm Elisity
items.summary: IonQ has completed its acquisition of Elisity, a zero trust security company, in an all stock transaction. IonQ's own announcement says it issued 1.15 billion US dollars of consideration in common stock at closing, with up to 150 million dollars more payable if Elisity meets revenue milestones through January 2028, and that Elisity's technology complements its post quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution work.
items.why: A quantum computing company is adding an operating security business to its revenue base.

items.headline: Zyxel patches zero day used to compromise nearly 1,000 network switches
items.summary: Zyxel has patched a zero day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches. BleepingComputer reports that attackers exploited it to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials.
items.why: Network switches are trusted infrastructure; stolen configurations hand attackers a map of the networks those switches protect.

items.headline: Google patches critical Android flaw that needs no user interaction
items.summary: Google's November security bulletin patches a critical flaw, CVE-2026-58868, that could let an attacker run code on a phone remotely without any user action. It affects Android 14 through 17, and the fix arrives at security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers distribute on their own schedules.
items.why: The gap between Google's patch and each maker's rollout is the window of exposure for most Android users.

items.headline: Google previews AlloyDB Express, a scale to zero PostgreSQL for developers and agents
items.summary: Google has announced a preview of AlloyDB Express, a version of AlloyDB for PostgreSQL designed for rapid testing and prototyping. It offers instant provisioning and scale to zero, aimed at development pipelines and coding agents that need short lived databases.
items.why: Databases are being reshaped around agent driven development, where environments spin up and down in minutes.

items.headline: Amazon S3 Tables can now migrate Hive tables to Iceberg for you
items.summary: AWS has added managed migration from Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg in Amazon S3 Tables. AWS says existing datasets can be converted with no pipelines to build and no compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.
items.why: Iceberg has become the default table format for lakehouse data, and managed migration removes the main barrier to switching.

items.headline: US voters decide 41 local data centre measures in the midterm elections
items.summary: Ballotpedia counted 41 local ballot measures on data centre policy across 10 states on November 3: 28 would limit development and 13 would facilitate it. In reported results, Edgewater, Florida voted to add a ban on new data centres to its city charter, Alhambra, California voted to prohibit data centres, and Harwood, North Dakota rejected its restrictive measure, the only one voted down in USA Today's tally of local results.
items.why: Local ballot outcomes now directly decide where large data centres can be built in the United States.

items.headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, a security model built to stay inside its authorised scope
items.summary: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a model for finding exploitable vulnerabilities and developing fixes, trained to stay within the scope researchers set. It scores 48.5% on ExploitGym, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber, and avoided out of scope services in 99.93% of alignment tests without deployment prompts. It already helped find 81 previously unknown high severity Firefox flaws, and it is initially available through the API and Codex to approved Daybreak Red customers.
items.why: Security models that can find flaws are only useful if they can be trusted not to wander, and this one pairs stronger exploit skills with measured restraint.

items.headline: Google ships Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with 15 second video and a 30% price cut
items.summary: Google made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generally available across the Gemini API and Google Cloud. It creates and edits video clips up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds, with multi turn conversational editing and stronger reference consistency. The price falls 30% from version 1.1, to $0.07 per second for 720p video.
items.why: Video generation is moving from short demos toward usable ad and product clips, with editing and pricing aimed at production use.

items.headline: Claude can now read your bank account, with read only access through Plaid
items.summary: Anthropic launched Personal Finance in Claude in beta, connecting the chatbot to bank and card accounts through Plaid. Claude can break down spending by category, say which bills remain before payday, and judge whether a large purchase is affordable, using up to two years of transaction history. Access is read only: Claude cannot move, manage or invest money, and it does not see banking passwords. The beta is rolling out this week to Claude Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the US.
items.why: AI assistants are moving from answering questions to acting on personal financial data, which makes read only access and clear limits the story.

items.headline: Quantinuum maps its Nexus platform toward a fault tolerant computer in 2029
items.summary: Quantinuum published a roadmap to grow Nexus, its platform as a service, into a developer platform for fault tolerant quantum applications, tracking hardware releases through Apollo, its planned universal fault tolerant computer in 2029. Releases will progressively automate error correction, resource management and deployment. Nexus already serves more than 200 organisations, up 45% in 2026, with job submissions up tenfold in the year to August 2026.
items.why: Quantum vendors are now competing on developer platforms, not only hardware, so applications built today can carry over to fault tolerant machines.

items.headline: IBM, Oak Ridge and AMD pair quantum hardware with supercomputing to advance error correction
items.summary: IBM, the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD launched a joint co-design platform for quantum error correction, combining quantum and high performance computing. The first deployment pairs IBM quantum computers, including the 120 qubit Nighthawk processor, with Oak Ridge's Umbra system, powered by AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen EPYC CPUs. The work supports the US Department of Energy goal of 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028.
items.why: Error correction needs classical computing at scale, and this platform tests quantum and supercomputing as one system rather than two separate tools.

items.headline: Azure Front Door gains generally available post quantum TLS key exchange
items.summary: Microsoft made configurable TLS key exchange policies generally available in Azure Front Door, including hybrid post quantum key exchange. The option is aimed at teams preparing for future cryptographic threats while keeping client compatibility.
items.why: Post quantum readiness is reaching production edge services, so teams can start the migration before quantum computers threaten current cryptography.

items.headline: Google donates its agent runtime stack to the CNCF as Agent Substrate hits 1.0
items.summary: Google donated three open source projects that started at Google, Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation after their acceptance into the CNCF Sandbox. Agent Substrate, which runs isolated agent environments, reached version 1.0 and is generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine, restoring idle agents in under 500 milliseconds at 10 times container density.
items.why: Agent infrastructure is getting the same neutral, open governance treatment Kubernetes got, so no single vendor controls how agents run at scale.

items.headline: OpenSSH ships emergency fix for a flaw that let long passwords bypass login on Alpine Linux
items.summary: OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 to fix a critical flaw in which a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long could log in to accounts with no password set, such as key only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers. The flaw affects systems where the server checks passwords without PAM, which is how Alpine's openssh-server package is built. Alpine published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16, and no attacks using the flaw have been reported.
items.why: A password check that accepts the wrong input is a serious failure, and Alpine's wide use in containers makes fast patching matter.

items.headline: FBI and CISA warn hackers are targeting refrigeration systems
items.summary: The FBI and CISA warned that hackers are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems worldwide, in a joint advisory with the US health, agriculture and transport departments. Attackers exploit unpatched or internet accessible temperature controllers to alter settings, which can spoil food, damage equipment and create fire hazards. The warning follows attacks on European refrigeration systems, including controllers at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets in October.
items.why: Cyberattacks on refrigeration reach beyond data theft into food safety and public health, so operators are urged to take controllers off the public internet.

items.headline: Horizon Quantum plans to buy error correction specialist Entropica Labs for $27 million
items.summary: Horizon Quantum signed a non-binding letter of intent to acquire Singapore based quantum software company Entropica Labs for about $27 million in Horizon Quantum Class A ordinary shares. Entropica Labs specialises in error correction and fault tolerance. The deal still needs due diligence, audits and definitive agreements.
items.why: Quantum software firms are consolidating around error correction, the capability every hardware maker needs before fault tolerant machines arrive.

items.headline: Agility Robotics lists on Nasdaq as humanoid robots face scrutiny over scale
items.summary: Agility Robotics, maker of the Digit humanoid robot, listed on the Nasdaq on November 5 through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company, becoming the first dedicated humanoid robot developer to trade publicly in the US. Digit robots already work at customer sites including GXO warehouses and a Schaeffler factory, and the next model, Digit 5, arrives in 2027 with 50 pound lifting and more than 20 hours of work per day. The company's filing shows $1.8 million of revenue in 2025 against a $140 million operating loss, and notes humanoid robots remain unproven at scale.
items.why: A public listing tests whether investors will fund humanoid robots before the market proves itself, and Agility's numbers show how early that bet still is.

items.headline: OpenAI drops NDAs with public officials for its data centre projects
items.summary: OpenAI published a National Community Compact and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint setting out commitments for future compute campuses it owns and operates, including paying the full cost of the electricity it uses and publishing the jobs it expects to create. It will not use non-disclosure agreements with public officials, allowing only narrow protections for security information, trade secrets or proprietary information. The announcement follows midterm votes in which US voters decided local data centre measures.
items.why: Data centre deals have drawn scrutiny over secrecy and local costs, and OpenAI is putting its community terms in writing rather than leaving them to negotiation.

items.headline: Perplexity launches always on work agents called Teammates
items.summary: Perplexity has launched Teammates, always on AI agents built for work that can take on different roles in a workspace at the same time. Each Teammate works from its own thread in the Perplexity app and can draw on existing projects, skills and memory, and users can talk to them in Slack. Access is limited to the $200 a month Max plan, and chief executive Aravind Srinivas said on X that he sees organisations eventually having hundreds of Teammates working for each person.
items.why: Work agents are moving from single chatbots to teams of agents with their own roles, and Perplexity is charging a premium for the shift.

items.headline: Meta Muse can now build custom spaces from a description
items.summary: Meta has added spaces to its Muse assistant, letting users describe an app such as a shopping hub, a school dashboard or a trivia game and have Muse build it. Connected apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable and Notion let Muse keep the details in a space current in the background, and users can tick items off, add notes and place spaces in the sidebar or on a schedule. Meta also said Active Memory and Active Focus, capabilities from its Muse Wonder model, are coming to the Muse app and the Meta AI chatbot.
items.why: Assistants are turning into personalised workspaces that stay current on their own, which raises the bar for what a chatbot is expected to do.

items.headline: Cognition ships a cheaper coding model but keeps its weights private
items.summary: Cognition has released SWE-2 Flash, a coding model it says costs a fifth as much as its larger SWE-2 model and generates tokens about three times faster. Flash is built on Thinking Machines Lab’s open weight Inkling Small model, yet Cognition is keeping its own weights private, citing cybersecurity concerns. On Cognition’s own figures, Flash scored 20% on Terminal Bench 4.0 against 0.9% for the base model, and 89.9% on SWE Bench Pro v2 Hard, close to SWE-2’s 90.6%.
items.why: A model built on an open base with closed weights tests how far openness extends in practice, and whether cheaper coding models can match their larger siblings.

items.headline: AI assisted proof settles a 2008 question about quantum speedups
items.summary: A proof by David Turturean of Physical Superintelligence has settled the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, open since 2008, which asks when quantum computers can gain dramatic advantages over classical machines. The proof shows that for yes or no questions on most randomly generated inputs, a classical algorithm can estimate a quantum algorithm’s answer without needing vastly more reads of the input, so large speedups need structure in the problem. The proof was found by an AI research system using a non public Anthropic model on the third day of a run, then checked in the Lean proof assistant and reviewed by researchers.
items.why: It draws a clearer line around where quantum advantage can come from, pointing algorithm research toward problems with structure worth exploiting.

items.headline: UK announces fresh funding to speed up quantum commercialisation
items.summary: The UK government and UK Research and Innovation have announced new funding to speed up quantum commercialisation, including £138 million for quantum sensing procurement across government, £12 million for a national commercialisation skills centre and £35 million for quantum networking testbeds. The skills centre will be run by the UK Quantum SuperConnector, a partnership led by Imperial College London with Bristol, Cambridge, Glasgow and Oxford. A UKRI review of £300 million invested between 2014 and 2024 found it helped create more than 2,000 skilled jobs, supported 74 spinout companies and attracted £482 million in private investment.
items.why: Public money is now aimed at turning research into products and jobs, and the UK is measuring a decade of funding by the companies and skills it produced.

items.headline: Google hands gVisor and its agent stack to the CNCF
items.summary: Google is donating gVisor, Agent Substrate and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, putting its AI agent infrastructure under neutral governance. gVisor, open sourced by Google in 2018, runs a lightweight kernel in user space to intercept system calls, adding isolation between containers and the host system, and is used by Anthropic and OpenAI to run untrusted code. Agent Substrate 1.0, now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine, lets agents pause when idle and resume without rebuilding their runtime, while OpenRL coordinates reinforcement learning training on a user’s own Kubernetes setup.
items.why: Sandboxing is becoming core infrastructure for agents that run untrusted code, and neutral ownership is Google’s bid to make its stack the default.

items.headline: Cursor will now publish AI built apps to a live URL
items.summary: Cursor has added fully managed deployment, letting its cloud agents take an AI generated app from a description to a live, shareable web address without the user setting up infrastructure. Cursor handles hosting, database provisioning and sign in, runs security checks for exposed credentials and secrets before publishing, and builds on Vercel for Platforms. The feature is available on all paid Cursor plans with cloud agents enabled, and targets internal business apps as well as personal projects.
items.why: Coding tools are closing the gap between generating an app and shipping it, which makes deployment skill less of a gate for new builders.

items.headline: Chainalysis breach exposed credentials for all customers
items.summary: Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis says an attack on its systems exposed usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all of its customers. The company, whose customers include law enforcement, government agencies and financial institutions, has taken its login portal and several products offline, including Reactor and its transaction screening tools. It says it has found no evidence that investigation data was accessed, and all users will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys before regaining access.
items.why: A breach at a firm that traces crypto crime puts its own customers’ access at risk, and the shutdown shows how much trust the service carries.

items.headline: QNAP warns hackers are breaching NAS devices through Plex
items.summary: QNAP says hackers are exploiting the Plex2Shell chain of four flaws in Plex Media Server to compromise its network attached storage devices, and it has received multiple reports of suspected breaches. The company urges users to update Plex Media Server to version 1.43.3.10861 through the QNAP App Center, noting that its own operating systems are not affected. Users with an exposed Plex server should treat their device and stored content as compromised, check for signs of intrusion and reinstall the operating system rather than only updating.
items.why: A media app flaw is reaching into home and small business storage, and updating alone will not clear an attack that has already landed.

items.headline: IQM revenue up 51 percent as backlog passes €100 million
items.summary: IQM Quantum Computers reported third quarter revenue of €8.86 million, up 50.7 percent on a year earlier, and an order backlog of €102.5 million after booking €42.2 million in new orders during the quarter. The Finnish company reaffirmed full year revenue guidance of €42 million to €47 million and closed its largest contract to date, a €33 million deal with the LUMI AI Factory. It also sold its first system in South America and a second system in Japan.
items.why: Order books are growing faster than revenue for a quantum hardware maker, which is the clearest signal yet that buyers are committing real money.

items.headline: Protesters enter Microsoft data centre site in Amsterdam
items.summary: About 100 protesters entered the construction site of a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, according to Reuters, in a protest against three 85 metre towers planned for the outskirts of the city. Amsterdam has banned new data centres until 2030, but the project dates to 2016 and proceeds as planned, with Microsoft as sole tenant. It is the latest in a week of actions against data centre building, after voters in the United States rejected data centre development in local ballots earlier in the week.
items.why: Data centre building is meeting organised local resistance in Europe as well as the US, and older approvals are letting projects proceed despite new bans.

items.headline: US midterm results put data centre building under pressure
items.summary: Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the United States midterm elections on Tuesday, a result that carries direct consequences for data centre building. Voters decided 41 ballot measures about data centres across 10 states, and all but one went against data centre development, with Harwood in North Dakota the only exception. Texas, one of the largest data centre hubs, saw Democrats win races up and down the ballot, and candidates from both parties had campaigned against data centre expansion in several states.
items.why: Election results now shape where data centres can be built, turning local planning fights into a national question for the AI buildout.

items.headline: DeepMind AI agents find two weaknesses in retired 1024-bit RSA
items.summary: Google DeepMind says AI agents working under human supervision found two weaknesses in legacy 1024-bit RSA encryption, a key size the industry retired years ago. In a sandbox test, the agents reproduced a signature forgery on a solved benchmark key using 3.5 times less CPU time, and a new algorithm improved on the previous best method by roughly 1,600 times in theoretical estimates for short fingerprints, while a second result cuts the average cost of factoring each additional 1024-bit key by about 30 times. DeepMind states modern 2048-bit and larger keys are unaffected and no live systems were touched.
items.why: AI agents are now doing original cryptanalysis in weeks, so hardness assumptions need continuous re-testing rather than being treated as fixed.

items.headline: Thinking Machines Lab ships Inkling 2 Small, with open weights promised next week
items.summary: Thinking Machines Lab has released Inkling 2 Small, a mixture-of-experts model with 594 billion total parameters and 17 billion active per token, which takes text and image input. The lab reports a score of 31 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and says the model is built for long autonomous coding and research tasks. It is available now through the lab's Tinker platform with closed weights, and the lab says it intends to release the full weights under an Apache 2.0 licence next week, after external safety testing and red-teaming.
items.why: The model is built for hours-long autonomous coding work, and its weights stay closed until safety testing finishes, so the open release is conditional rather than immediate.

items.headline: IBM unveils Quantum System Two at the University of Chicago
items.summary: IBM, the University of Chicago, the State of Illinois and the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park have unveiled an IBM Quantum System Two in Chicago, the company's first quantum computer in Illinois. The system runs on IBM's Nighthawk processor, a 120-qubit chip, and is hosted at the university's Hyde Park Labs. It anchors the National Quantum Algorithm Center, where researchers from universities, labs and companies work on practical quantum applications, and will move to the new Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park campus once it is built.
items.why: Putting a 120-qubit system on a university campus gives Illinois researchers local hardware for algorithm work instead of remote cloud access.

items.headline: Oxford team simulates Aharonov-Bohm effect with two trapped ions
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Oxford have simulated the Aharonov-Bohm effect in a lattice gauge theory using a hybrid trapped-ion quantum computer, in a study published in Nature Physics. Two trapped ions formed a loop with two paths, and entangling the qubits that encode the magnetic flux changed whether a particle could tunnel between sites. When the entangled qubits encoded a nonzero flux, the two paths cancelled out and tunnelling stopped entirely, showing the simulation captures how flux affects particle motion.
items.why: Simulating gauge theories with matter and flux together moves quantum simulation closer to the physics behind particle interactions and exotic materials.

items.headline: AWS makes Kiro bots generally available in Kiro Crew
items.summary: Amazon Web Services has made Kiro bots generally available in Kiro Crew, its open-source multi-agent development environment. Each bot is a named, long-running agent with its own durable memory, kept in a notes file the developer can edit, and its own tools and permissions for one standing job such as triaging tickets or watching builds. A bot runs parallel worker sessions and can ask for more tools, but cannot take them without developer approval, and bots cannot delegate work to each other.
items.why: Giving each agent its own memory and a standing job shifts developers from carrying context between sessions to handing off whole processes.

items.headline: SageMaker Inference now supports NVIDIA multi-instance GPU partitioning
items.summary: Amazon SageMaker Inference now supports GPU partitioning with NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU, which splits one GPU into hardware-isolated partitions. Each partition can run a different model, or take a right-sized fraction of a newer accelerator, so teams can pack more models onto one card. The feature is aimed at raising GPU utilisation for model endpoints.
items.why: Splitting one GPU into isolated partitions lets teams run more models per accelerator and cut inference cost.

items.headline: Claude Code settings files leak passwords and keys in public GitHub repos
items.summary: Security researchers at Apiiro found 1,122 public copies of Claude Code's settings file holding at least one secret, including database passwords, cloud keys and tokens. The file, .claude/settings.local.json, records commands a user approved with 'don't ask again', word for word, so passwords typed into a command are saved in plain text. Apiiro counted 1,379 secrets in current copies and 2,539 in total across 1,994 repositories once older versions, forks and shared settings files are included, and says the fix starts with rotating every exposed credential.
items.why: Secrets saved in agent settings files leak into public repos, so teams need to treat agent folders like credential stores and scan their history.

items.headline: French bank Arkéa hit by heist of up to $133 million through a service provider
items.summary: French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa was hit by a cyberattack in which the attacker used the bank's own account to send fraudulent transactions to other banks. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT estimated up to 118 million euros ($133 million) was taken and converted into stablecoins, while the bank would only confirm the order of magnitude. The bank says customer assets were not affected, the incident is closed and under control, and it is working with police to establish how the attacker got in through a service provider's platform.
items.why: A bank's own account was used to move funds through a service provider, showing third-party access is now a direct route to the money.

items.headline: Microsoft warns agentic AI framework ARTEX is being used against banks
items.summary: Microsoft says the financially motivated group it tracks as Storm-3358 began targeting financial organisations in October using ARTEX, an agentic AI offensive framework. The group, which Microsoft describes as Cambodia-based and focused on financial targets in Southeast Asia, uses ARTEX agents to scan public systems, exploit flaws such as anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery, and install remote access trojans. Microsoft has published indicators of compromise and detections, and says defenders need AI-assisted investigation to match attacks that move at machine speed.
items.why: Agentic frameworks let attackers scan, exploit and move laterally at machine speed, so defence has to detect and respond at the same pace.

items.headline: IonQ posts record $173.8 million quarter and raises full-year guidance
items.summary: IonQ reported record third-quarter revenue of $173.8 million, up 336% year over year, its sixth consecutive record quarter. The company raised full-year 2026 revenue guidance to between $505 million and $515 million, from $450 million to $460 million, and said its backlog reached $1.2 billion. Net income was $564.0 million, or $1.42 per share, reflecting a non-cash mark-to-market gain on warrants.
items.why: Six straight record quarters and a $1.2 billion backlog show demand for quantum systems is outrunning supply.

items.headline: Quantinuum revenue up 233% to $9.1 million as it raises its outlook
items.summary: Quantinuum reported third-quarter revenue of $9.1 million, up 233% year over year, and raised its full-year 2026 revenue outlook to between $31 million and $34 million, from $28 million to $32 million. The company also reported a net loss of $118 million and cash of $1.94 billion, and said it signed its largest cloud agreement to date, a multi-year deal with a global financial institution. On hardware, its Helios system reached 99.9995% logical memory fidelity in October, which the company says is within the accuracy range targeted for its Apollo machine.
items.why: Revenue up 233% with a raised outlook shows trapped-ion systems are converting research progress into paying customers.

items.headline: UK regulator launches quantum group to test machine learning against financial crime
items.summary: The UK Financial Conduct Authority has set up a Quantum Experimentation Group to test whether quantum machine learning can improve detection of money laundering and fraud. The group launches in the first quarter of 2027 and brings together financial firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories. Participants will test methods on a synthetic dataset the FCA created, since banks cannot share real transaction records, and firms can register interest by 31 December 2026.
items.why: A regulator testing quantum machine learning on synthetic fraud data gives financial firms a supervised path to try quantum tools.

items.headline: Apple pushes Siri toward agentic tasks, report says
items.summary: Bloomberg reports that Apple chief executive John Ternus is pressing AI chief Craig Federighi to speed up the Siri roadmap and deliver an assistant that can act on its own, rivalling OpenAI's Dots and Meta's Muse. Fine-grained control of Apple's own apps, such as editing photos and organising Safari tabs, is reported to arrive with iOS 27.3, while control of third-party apps, such as placing a food order or booking a table, is reported to follow in the spring. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman writes that Siri could become more like an agent as early as next year.
items.why: Siri is the assistant built into Apple's devices, so turning it into an assistant that carries out multi-step tasks changes what phone assistants are expected to do.

items.headline: Nvidia board opens independent review of chief executive after spy reports
items.summary: Nvidia's board of directors said it is opening an independent investigation into chief executive Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who US officials believe was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. The board said it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang supports the review and will cooperate. The New York Times reported last month on the relationship, which Huang later described as romantic in a memo to staff. Megaspeed, a Nvidia customer, is under a Commerce Department investigation into alleged smuggling of AI chips to China.
items.why: The review sits where chip export controls meet corporate governance, and its outcome shapes how Nvidia handles foreign-intelligence risk at the top of the company.

items.headline: Elvis and Eminem rights holders sue Suno over AI music clones
items.summary: Rights holders for Elvis Presley's music and the publisher of some of Eminem's biggest records have sued AI music company Suno, saying it generates music and lyrics that mimic the artists. The Presley suit says Suno violated Tennessee's ELVIS Act, which bars AI companies from cloning a singer's voice. Suno says it prohibits unauthorised use of an artist's work, blocks prompts naming specific artists, and screens uploads for misuse. The suits follow similar claims by Jason Isbell and others in September and add to cases already brought by Sony and Universal Music Group.
items.why: The cases test whether voice and likeness laws cover AI-generated imitations, a question that decides how music AI tools can be built and sold.

items.headline: Perplexity's Teammates keep AI agents working between sessions
items.summary: Perplexity has launched Teammates, a system that coordinates several AI agents which remember where past sessions left off and keep working without a new prompt. Shared project state lives in Git, with each project in its own repository and each agent working in a separate sandbox. Perplexity says fewer than 2% of agent submissions are rejected for being based on outdated state, with median submission latency under 1.7 seconds. Teammates is available first on the web for Perplexity Max subscribers, with iOS support planned.
items.why: Agents that keep working after a tab closes move AI tools from answering questions toward carrying out multi-step work on their own.

items.headline: Iris Ohyama breach may have exposed data of 7.7 million people
items.summary: Japanese manufacturer Iris Ohyama said personal information belonging to about 7.7 million people may have been exposed after unauthorised access to a third-party cloud service used by its Iris Plaza online store. The company said the impact reaches up to 5.8 million registered and former members and 1.9 million non-members. Names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth and passwords may have been exposed, though passwords for active members were stored encrypted and card data was not in the affected service. As of November 5 the company had received no reports of misuse, and Japan's privacy regulator and police were notified on October 29.
items.why: A breach through a supplier's cloud service shows customer data can be exposed even when the retailer's own systems are not the entry point.

items.headline: Riverlane cuts surface-code logical errors with data-driven decoder fix
items.summary: Riverlane has demonstrated a method that finds unmodelled correlated errors directly from syndrome measurement data and folds them into the detector error models used to decode surface-code qubits. The augmented models cut logical error rates by up to 75% in simulations and by 14% on Google's published superconducting hardware data. The approach stays compatible with fast graph-based decoders such as PyMatching, which existing error-correction pipelines already use.
items.why: Better decoding from measured noise, rather than from theory alone, moves error-corrected quantum computing forward without waiting on new hardware.

items.headline: A decision framework for moving autonomous agents from Lambda to EKS
items.summary: A senior QA engineer at Amazon describes an autonomous agent that reads test failures, files structured bug reports and catches regressions, running on AWS Lambda for one team at under $5 a month and about 200 invocations a month, saving 8 to 10 hours a week. Scaling the same agent to 50 teams changes the workload from stateless events to long-running, multi-tenant work with shared state and API contention, and the piece sets out when to move to EKS Auto Mode: when a workload needs persistent state, cross-tenant analysis, GPU bursts, namespace isolation and central rate limiting together. At 50 teams the EKS setup is put at roughly $200 to $250 a month in total.
items.why: The piece gives teams a concrete test for moving agents off serverless, which matters as agent workloads grow from one team to many.

items.headline: Docusign turns AI coding tools into an engineering operating model
items.summary: Docusign says all of its more than 1,100 engineers are now onboarded to and actively using AI coding tools, after early adoption stalled at 49% of engineers and an 18% productivity gain levelled off. The company credits a six-person Eng AI Champions team and about 75 AI Multipliers embedded in teams, with active usage reaching 93% within two months of the Multipliers starting, and lines of code updated per developer up about 52% from the starting point, though the article notes that volume alone does not prove faster delivery. Internal tools include Kody for coding, Chronicle for observability and DocuWiki for documentation, brought together in Krew, where teams build agents for recurring work under human review; no code enters the system unreviewed.
items.why: Docusign's numbers show the hard part of AI coding tools is not the rollout but the operating model around them, a lesson other engineering teams are now working through.
